query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: HEA nanoparticles composed of five or more metals will maintain their single‐phase, chemically homogeneous structure across the high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric operating range (473–1923 K) when the constituent metals possess similar melting points and diffusion kinetics, because uniform atomic mobility preserves configurational entropy. In contrast, nanoparticles with significant mismatches in these properties will experience differential diffusion rates that drive elemental segregation and phase transformation.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles with five or more metals in near‐equal atomic ratios, crystallized as a uniform single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Synthesize two sets of HEA nanoparticles: one set using metals chosen for closely matched melting points and similar atomic diffusivities (controlled group) and a comparison set with metals selected to have larger disparities in melting points and/or diffusion kinetics. Both sets are then exposed to catalytic/thermoelectric operating conditions (temperature range 473–1923 K) under identical controlled atmospheres.
generation.conditions: High-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions maintained under inert or well-controlled atmospheres, over extended durations within the 473–1923 K range, to isolate the impact of inter-element diffusional mismatches on phase stability.
generation.structural_mediator: Differences in the diffusion kinetics of constituent metals governed by their intrinsic melting points and activation barriers for diffusion.
generation.mechanism: When metals have similar melting points and diffusion barriers, the uniform/sluggish diffusion maintains high configurational entropy and prevents local atomic rearrangements, preserving the single-phase structure. Conversely, significant mismatches lead to differential diffusion, thereby destabilizing the homogeneous solid solution and promoting phase segregation or localized ordering.
generation.predicted_outcome: The nanoparticles synthesized with well-matched elemental properties will retain a uniform, single-phase structure (as characterized by XRD, TEM, and EDS) after high-temperature exposure. In the mismatched set, evidence of phase segregation, compositional gradients, or secondary phase formation will develop relative to the initial homogeneous state.
generation.baseline: Uniform, single-phase HEA nanoparticles with equimolar (or near-equimolar) composition before high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold under high-temperature catalytic/thermoelectric operating conditions (473–1923 K) where oxidative or substrate interactions are minimized, and the primary variable influencing stability is inter-element diffusion driven by melting point and kinetic disparities.
generation.uncertainty: While the role of uniformly matched melting points and diffusion kinetics is central to the hypothesis, uncertainties remain regarding how additional factors such as local lattice distortions or minor fluctuations in the microstructure might influence the kinetics of phase segregation at the extreme upper range of operating temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA nanoparticles: one with metals selected for similar melting points and diffusion kinetics (controlled group) and one with intentionally larger mismatches (comparison group). Subject both sets to extended high-temperature catalytic/thermoelectric conditions (473–1923 K) under identical, inert atmospheres. Pre- and post-treatment characterizations will be performed using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for morphological and phase uniformity assessment, and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping for elemental distribution.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the controlled and mismatched sets exhibit similar retention of a single-phase, chemically homogeneous structure, or if the controlled set (with well-matched melting points/diffusion kinetics) unexpectedly shows significant phase segregation or compositional inhomogeneity, the hypothesis will be falsified.

decision.trend: Early work on high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles has focused on demonstrating that single‐phase solid solutions can be synthesized and maintained under catalytic conditions. For example, PMC6728353 showed that by carefully tuning elemental ratios (e.g., Co/Mo in a quinary system) one can achieve robust catalytic activity, implying that careful compositional control helps forestall phase separation. Later, PMC7069714 employed computational prescreening and rapid high‐temperature synthesis to yield nanoparticles with excellent thermal stability, hinting that high synthesis temperatures and ensuing short processing times can preserve the solid solution state even in multi‐element systems. More recently, PMC10466320 explored sub‐nanometric HEA clusters where structural reversibility under oxidative/reductive cycling was observed, further suggesting that atomic-level mixing and local kinetics are critical to maintain phase integrity. However, none have systematically isolated the role of inter-element diffusivity differences or melting point mismatches in governing stability over the full, high temperature catalytic/thermoelectric operating range.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved how the interplay between intrinsic elemental properties (e.g. differences in melting points, bonding strengths, and atomic mobilities) controls whether a multi‐element nanoparticle retains its single-phase structure and chemical homogeneity when exposed to extended high temperature regimes (473–1923 K). In particular, while overall configurational entropy is known to stabilize the solid solution at synthesis, the specific kinetic factors that might lead to elemental segregation or phase transformations under operating conditions have not been isolated.
decision.lever: Designing experiments that control the degree of melting point and diffusivity mismatches among constituent elements
decision.why: A rational next step is to synthesize two sets of HEA nanoparticles: one in which constituent metals are selected to have closely matched melting points and similar diffusion kinetics, and another with intentionally greater disparities. By holding all other synthesis parameters constant and subjecting these samples to catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions from 473–1923 K, one can directly test whether minimizing diffusion mismatch governs structural and chemical stability. This controlled comparative approach directly builds upon the trend of tuning compositional parameters for improved catalytic performance while addressing the remaining open question regarding high temperature kinetic effects.
